p.t: Almost everyone has postponed an important task while doing something far less useful instead: tidying a desk, checking messages or watching just one more video. For a long time, this habit was seen as a simple lack of discipline. Recent research, however, suggests that the question of why we delay tasks we know are important is more complex and more interesting than it first appears.

Psychologists define procrastination as the voluntary delay of an intended action despite expecting to be worse off because of the delay. This definition separates it from strategic waiting, such as delaying a purchase until prices fall. The key element is irrationality: the procrastinator knows that the delay is likely to cause harm, yet chooses it anyway.

One influential explanation focuses on emotion rather than time management. According to this view, people put off tasks that make them feel anxious, bored or insecure, because postponing them brings immediate emotional relief. The relief, however, is temporary, and the unfinished task often returns with even stronger negative feelings, which makes further delay more likely.

A study carried out at a Canadian university illustrates this point. Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before their first exam procrastinated significantly less before the second one. By reducing the guilt attached to the task, self-forgiveness appears to have weakened the emotional cycle that keeps people avoiding their work.

Not all delay, however, is harmful. Some researchers distinguish between ordinary procrastinators and so-called active procrastinators, who deliberately postpone work because they believe they perform better under pressure. Unlike ordinary procrastinators, these individuals usually meet their deadlines and do not report the same levels of stress.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the solution to procrastination may lie less in better calendars than in better emotional habits. Planning tools can certainly help, but as long as a task remains a source of anxiety, people are likely to find creative ways of avoiding it.

p.t: Twenty years ago, most clothing shops changed their collections four times a year, following the seasons. Today, some brands introduce new designs every week, and customers have come to expect a constant stream of cheap, fashionable clothes. This transformation has changed not only how people shop but also how they think about clothing itself.

The term 'fast fashion' refers to a business model in which retailers copy trends from fashion shows and celebrity culture very quickly and produce them at low cost. Rather than being designed to last for years, these garments are intended to be worn for a short time and then replaced by the next trend.

Several developments made this model possible. First, global supply chains allowed companies to move production to countries where labour was cheap. Second, improved logistics reduced the time between design and delivery from months to weeks. Finally, social media created a culture in which being photographed in the same outfit twice became, for some, a social embarrassment.

The environmental costs of this system are considerable. Producing a single cotton T-shirt requires large amounts of water, and synthetic fabrics release tiny plastic fibres every time they are washed. Moreover, because the clothes are so cheap, a large share of them is thrown away after being worn only a few times.

Defenders of fast fashion argue, however, that the industry has made stylish clothing affordable for people on low incomes, who were once excluded from following fashion. They also point out that the factories involved provide millions of jobs, many of them for women, in developing economies.

Whether the industry can become sustainable may therefore depend less on the good intentions of individual shoppers than on regulation. Laws that require companies to take responsibility for their products after they are sold could change the economics of fast fashion more effectively than appeals to consumers' consciences.

sempo.title: Should universities allow AI writing tools?

sch.t: Banning AI writing tools is simply unenforceable: students will use them at home whatever the rules say. Instead of fighting technology, universities should rethink assessment. Oral examinations, in-class writing and portfolios that show how a piece of work developed over time make it much harder to submit work that is not one's own, while still allowing students to benefit from AI as a learning aid.

Writing is not just a way of reporting ideas; it is one of the main ways in which we form them. When students let a machine produce their first drafts, they skip the stage at which an argument actually takes shape. I would allow AI for revising a finished text, for example to check grammar, but drafting should remain the student's own work, at least in the first years of university.

Whatever policy universities choose, it must not depend on AI detectors. These programs are far less reliable than their makers claim, and they are particularly likely to flag texts written by non-native speakers of English, whose simpler sentence structures resemble machine-generated text. Failing a student on the basis of such software would be deeply unfair.

The ethical question is not whether students use AI but whether they are honest about it. A student who openly explains how a tool helped them is no more a cheat than one who asks a friend to read a draft. What universities should require is transparency: every assignment should include a short statement describing whether and how AI was used.

radar.title: A SHORT HISTORY OF PAPER MONEY
p: Before paper money existed, trade depended on coins made of metal. These were valuable and widely trusted, but they were also heavy, which made them impractical for merchants who had to travel long distances.

The first paper notes appeared in China during the Tang dynasty. Merchants left their heavy coins with trusted agents and received written certificates instead, which they could later exchange for the coins in another city.
By the eleventh century, the government of the Song dynasty had taken control of printing these notes, partly to stop private traders from issuing too many of them.
Marco Polo, who travelled to China in the thirteenth century, described with astonishment how the emperor's paper was accepted as payment in every part of the empire.
In Europe, a Swedish bank issued the continent's first banknotes in 1661, at a time when the country's copper coins were so large and heavy that they were difficult to use in everyday trade.
Printing paper money, however, brought new dangers. When governments produced notes faster than their economies grew, prices rose sharply, a process economists call inflation.
To build public trust, many countries later promised that their notes could be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold. In various forms, this arrangement lasted until the 1970s.
Today, digital payments are gradually replacing cash in some countries, and some economists predict that physical banknotes may one day become little more than collectors' items.
